source.title: Neural Anisotropy Directions
source.authors: Guillermo Ortiz-Jiménez; Apostolos Modas; Seyed-Mohsen Moosavi-Dezfooli; P. Frossard

record.tranche_reason: Tests how architectural directional bias affects generalization using synthetic linearly separable distributions and CIFAR-10 transformations; it does not test the claim versions’ specified interventions or measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on synthetic linearly separable distributions and modified CIFAR-10. It does not test random-label memorization, width sweeps, convolution-versus-fully-connected comparisons on images, optimizer or batch-size effects, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples.
record.test_reason: The study tests directional architectural bias, rather than any specified claim version. It does not compare random and natural labels, widths, optimizers, batch sizes, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or memorized-example removal. Its synthetic MLP and CNN experiments do not establish the convolution-versus-fully-connected comparison on natural image benchmarks described by V3.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors additionally emphasize that architecture can favor memorization even when a highly discriminative feature exists. NADs characterize feature preferences and help explain synthetic-task and CIFAR-10 results; the authors qualify their conclusions as mostly concerning fully separable, especially linearly separable, data.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies directional inductive bias using synthetic linearly separable distributions and CIFAR-10 feature manipulations; it does not reproduce the methods in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with the discriminative direction’s NAD index, noise level, and number of training samples; the CIFAR-10 flipped representation performs worse than the original. Removing pooling also equalizes performance across frequencies in a synthetic-data experiment, with values shown only in a figure.

fits_no_version.finding: CNN test accuracy on linearly separable synthetic distributions decreases as the discriminative direction moves to later NADs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alignment with an architecture's preferred directions affects generalization on linearly separable distributions.

fits_no_version.finding: Early-NAD class carriers produce low accuracy on clean CIFAR-10, whereas late-NAD carriers permit high clean-test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: NAD ordering helps predict which introduced shortcuts a CNN selects.

fits_no_version.finding: Flipping CIFAR-10 in each architecture's NAD basis lowers test accuracy despite approximately zero training error on both representations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An information-preserving representation change can impair CNN generalization by misaligning data with architectural bias.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix D.3 reports perfect generalization for a three-hidden-layer MLP across its NAD-parameterized synthetic tasks, while VGG11 generalizes to only a few. These are architecture-specific task sequences.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fully connected and convolutional architectures can differ substantially in directional bias on synthetic linearly separable tasks.

record.peer_reviewed: 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2020)
record.problems: The authors did not extensively tune hyperparameters and describe their comparisons as relative. Several accuracy results are presented only in figures. They state that the results mostly apply to fully separable, specifically linearly separable, data and leave non-separable datasets open.

untested.parts: Fixed random-label fitting versus natural-label generalization under the same architectures and training recipes, including chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Width increases beyond zero training error and their effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization on natural image benchmarks, local-connectivity contributions, learned sparse connections, and convolution-derived initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimization under limited or broader tuning and recovery through weight decay or optimizer switching.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout interventions, small-data and underfitting regimes, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and comparison with other measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: None of the listed versions receives a verdict. Synthetic labels are informative and noise-free, so fitting these datasets is not a random-label memorization test. Input-gradient covariance and optimization curvature are not magnitude-aware weight sharpness. No omitted result directly bearing on V1–V8 was identified.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural labels under the same recipe.
Widening one-hidden-layer ReLU networks past the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the stated local-connectivity comparisons.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization comparisons.
Large- versus small-batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout effects and the stated data-augmentation, dropout, and weight-decay comparisons.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the train-test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.

rows.subject: LeNet
rows.operation_detail: Trained on synthetic linearly separable distributions D(v) aligned with NAD directions; tested on the corresponding distribution.

conditions.value: NAD sequence; test accuracy decreases for higher NAD indices

rows.locator: Section 4.1, Figure 6; Appendix D.3, Figure S20
rows.note: The text describes accuracy decreasing monotonically across higher NAD indices; exact values are shown only in figures.
rows.check: The accuracy trend measures directional bias, not a listed version. Figure S20 concerns VGG11 and an MLP, not LeNet; retain Figure 6 as the main locator. A sweep across NAD indices cannot receive a single partial state for these versions.

conditions.value: NAD sequence; test accuracy decreases for higher NAD indices

rows.locator: Section 4.1, Figure 6; Appendix D.3, Figure S22
rows.note: The text describes accuracy decreasing with higher NAD indices and reports that with a large amount of training samples ResNet-18 can eventually generalize perfectly regardless of direction position.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-10 training data modified to include a class-discriminative carrier at paired NAD indices; evaluated on the original, unpoisoned CIFAR-10 test set.
rows.value: figure only; text describes it as very low
rows.note: The authors say the network ignores most generalizing features when carriers are placed at the first NADs; exact accuracy is figure-only.
rows.check: Low clean-test accuracy after adding an early-NAD carrier measures induced shortcut selection, not a listed version.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-10 training data modified to include a class-discriminative carrier at paired NAD indices; evaluated on the original, unpoisoned CIFAR-10 test set.

rows.note: The text reports near-perfect generalization for carriers at the end of the NAD sequence.
rows.check: High clean-test accuracy with late-NAD carriers measures resistance to the introduced shortcut, not a listed version. The qualitative value is supported by the prose.
